Europe’s diesel prices race ahead of US on export-ban risks
article:
(Sept 24): Diesel prices outside the US surged relative to American rates as the possibility of the Trump administration introducing an export ban rattled the market.

 

On Wednesday, Nymex heating oil, a near-identical product to diesel, closed at its smallest premium since the end of April to its European equivalent. The daily swing was the biggest since 2022, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sparked fears of shortages. It reversed partially on Thursday.

There’s still significant uncertainty about whether the US will bring in an export ban, but Energy Secretary Chris Wright told oil industry leaders to brace for possible curbs as retail prices surge domestically. President Donald Trump said he’d encouraged administration officials to consider restrictions. The European Union expressed concern about the prospect of a ban.

Any curbs would pile pressure on a global market that’s been beset by huge disruption already. Reduced flows from the Iran war, attacks by Yemen’s Houthi militants on Saudi refineries, and Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian plants have all cut the amount of fuel available significantly.

Fast-rising diesel prices are also becoming a hot topic for the world’s central bankers as they try to quell inflation.

“To have the largest free economy in the world talking about banning exports is just unprecedented,” David Bird, chief executive officer of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals said in an interview in London. “Refining margins are elevated but we hope this doesn’t last too long. It’s not good for anyone.”

See also: GOP senator calls for investigation into Trump family

The European Commission said on Thursday that it doesn’t currently see a shortage of diesel in the region, despite the high prices. An oil monitoring group within the bloc will meet next week to take stock of the situation, it added. Earlier this week, French President Emmanuel Macron called for the EU to relax some fuel quality rules in order to boost the amount of supply that’s available on the market.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) said this month that Europe still has significant emergency fuel reserves that it could release if necessary, another way in which it could act to put a lid on prices. About half of the refined fuel made available for release by the IEA’s member countries earlier this year was diesel.

In a sign of the issues facing some countries, Serbia’s government said on Thursday that it would release the equivalent of about 37,000 barrels of diesel from its emergency reserves. The country’s energy minister said it was to shield consumers from the global energy crisis, with demand set to be high next month.

See also: Supreme Court rejects Trump’s mail ballot curbs for US midterm election

If the US did move to ban exports, the focus would turn to where else in the world supply can be found. Shipments out of the Persian Gulf have also risen in recent weeks, traders said, though the pace of additional supplies would depend on refinery restarts.

China last month exported the most middle distillates, a type of fuel that includes diesel and jet fuel, in a year, according to Kpler data. The world’s largest crude importer has significant export capacity but those volumes can be limited by government quotas.

“Beyond price impacts, restricting exports would be a gift to our competitors,” a group of 30 US industry bodies, including American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, said in a letter to the White House on Wednesday. “If we pull back, other countries will step in, our influence will shrink, and our adversaries will gain ground.”

title: Addvalue’s shareholders give green light for proposed spin-off, proposed dilution
article:
Addvalue Technologies has been given the green light by its shareholders for its proposed spin-off and the proposed listing of its space connectivity business on the Nasdaq.

At the company’s extraordinary general meeting (EGM) on Sept 24, 99.99% of Addvalue Tech’s shareholders voted in favour of the proposed spin-off and the proposed listing.

Addvalue’s shareholders - 99.93% of them - also voted to approve the proposed dilution.

Addvalue has indicated previously that it plans to hold a post spin-off stake of at least 51%. It added that it intends to remain listed on the Singapore Exchange’s (SGX) Mainboard.

Maybank Securities’ Jarick Seet estimates that IDRS, the business to be spun off, will potentially generate US$15 million - US$20 million in FY2027 revenue and grow to US$25 million - US$30 million come FY2028.

CLSA’s Mahir Murtaza, in his initiation report on Aug 27, said the proposed Nasdaq listing should “further sharpen” catalysts by “allowing the business to be benchmarked directly agaginst global space-infrastructure peers”.

See also: Addvalue partners Viasat to deliver IDRS to US government fleets

Shares in Addvalue closed 0.5 cents lower or 2.63% down at 18.5 cents on Sept 24.

title: The Edge Singapore repeats Story of the Year and Hidden Gem wins at SGX Orb Awards 2026 yet again
article:
The Edge Singapore has maintained its winning streak in The Hidden Gem category at the latest iteration of the SGX Orb Awards, scoring a seventh straight win at the annual financial journalism awards organised by SGX Group.

Senior writer Kevin Tan won for his story “Men with a vision” (Issue 1240, May 18), where he spoke with Mainboard-listed Mencast’s group executive chairman and CEO Glenndle Sim on AI and additive manufacturing taking marine engineering company to the next level.

Tan beat out four other nominees, including The Edge Singapore’s senior writers, Lin Daoyi and Teo Zheng Long, who had coverage on Oiltek and iX Biopharma, respectively.

“Since The Edge Singapore started its publication back in 2002, we have kept a clear focus on our coverage of Singapore-listed companies that are of interest to the investment community. Winning yet another Hidden Gem story award is clear validation of our team's efforts featuring the well-deserved small and medium caps that make up the core of our market ecosystem,” says Chan Chao Peh, editor-in-chief of The Edge Singapore.

See also: From 2025: The Edge Singapore repeats Story of the Year, Hidden Gem wins at SGX Orb Awards

“As the Value Unlock efforts get underway, our team at The Edge Singapore is on a lookout to help tell the stories of many more well deserving home grown companies,” adds Chan.

The Edge Singapore also picked up the top prize for Story of the Year. “Is there a place for insurance in your portfolio” (Issue 1224, Jan 26) by associate editor Felicia Tan and senior writer Lin beat out two other nominees in this category, including Kevin’s story, “Down but not out” (Issue 1251, Aug 3), on the Chinese economy.

See also: More Singapore residents target more than $1 mil and retirement in their 40s: CIMB-NTU study

The Edge Singapore has won the Story of the Year prize at six of the award’s nine editions. Executive editor Goola Warden won the top prize last year with her cover story on Singapore’s strong currency leading to translation effects for listcos with overseas operations. Senior writer Nicole Lim won the 2024 award with a cover story on the creator economy.

"Insurance is a key piece in anybody's financial literacy level. This story, based on Felicia's extensive reporting, has hopefully helped bring more insights to this issue," says Chan.

The other nominee in this category was Ulrica Lin of Lianhe Zaobao, who wrote a story on common misconceptions about SpaceX’s IPO.

In total, The Edge Singapore scored seven nominations across three of the five award categories. Now in its ninth edition, this year’s SGX Orb Awards saw the addition of a special category — The Value Equation — which honours stories that look at how shareholder value is created and realised in Singapore’s stock market.

The Fifth Person’s Kenji Tay won for his coverage on Boustead Singapore and how it turns time into an asset. Other nominees in this category include Kevin’s story, “Singapore’s start-up ecosystem needs more than growth capital to succeed” (Issue 1240, May 18), which talks about Singapore’s capital market ecosystem and its increased attention from policymakers lately.

The Straits Times’ story, How well do you know the Singapore stock market? Won in the An Experiential Treat category, beating The Business Times’ article on imagining the benchmark Straits TImes Index (STI) at 10,000 points, as well as The Business Times’ article on Singapore’s large silver vault.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Dawn Cher of SG Budget Babe won #TheGoTo award, which honours digital platforms focused on financial education, beating The Financial Coconut’s Chills with TFC and Mediacorp’s Money Mind programme.

This year’s submissions were reviewed by a panel of judges: Eleanor Seet, president and head of Asia ex-Japan at Amova Asset Management; Jane Martinson, Marjorie Deane Professor of Financial Journalism at City, University of London; Olivier Fines, head of advocacy and policy research, EMEA at CFA Institute; Shane Chesson, founding partner of Openspace Capital; and Vis Nayar, CIO at Eastspring Investments.

Teo Ai June, head of marketing and communications at SGX Group, says financial markets are increasingly interconnected, and strong journalism helps audiences make sense of the forces shaping them. “The strongest stories cut through the complexity, challenge assumptions and show why developments matter beyond a single market or moment. The SGX Orb Awards celebrates the people who bring that clarity, insight and fresh perspectives to financial markets.”

title: Qualcomm renews licensing pact with Apple starting in 2027
article:
(Sept 24): Qualcomm Inc said it has renewed its global licensing pact with Apple Inc, effective in April 2027, ensuring the iPhone maker will remain a key customer in the near term.

“We are pleased to extend the Apple license agreement,” said John Han, the Qualcomm executive vice-president in charge of licensing. The length of the new agreement was not included in the statement on Thursday announcing the renewal.

Shares of Qualcomm pared earlier declines before markets opened in New York on Thursday. Apple’s stock was little changed.

The chipmaker, which is the largest maker of smartphone processors, gets licensing revenue from handset makers based on the number of units shipped. Apple is Qualcomm’s largest customer — accounting for more than a fifth of revenue, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

The two companies entered a licensing agreement in 2019, capping off a protracted legal battle over billions of dollars in licensing fees.

Since then, Apple has gradually been building its own cellular modems into recent iPhones to lessen its dependence on outside suppliers, an effort that began with the iPhone 16e in 2025. The company has said its latest in-house modem, the C2, delivers “groundbreaking efficiency” that prolongs battery life. It also supports faster millimetre-wave 5G connectivity in the US. This year’s iPhone 18 Pro line-up mostly uses the C2, with one exception: The 18 Pro Max in the US has a Qualcomm modem.

See also: Oracle cites ‘force majeure’ to shield itself on controversial data centre — Bloomberg

Qualcomm has been getting squeezed more than expected by a smartphone slump. The company, which outsources production of its chips, said it’s passing along some of its cost increases to customers. That will help profit margins recover over time, it has said. Memory-chip shortages — fuelled by runaway demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computers — have forced Qualcomm customers including Apple to produce fewer phones.

title: Oracle cites ‘force majeure’ to shield itself on controversial data centre — Bloomberg
article:
(Sept 24): Oracle Corp is moving to shield itself from racking up expenses on a massive data centre being built in New Mexico, adding a fresh wrinkle to a project beset by opposition and regulatory setbacks.

The technology giant sent the project’s developer, a unit of Blue Owl Capital Inc, a notice citing force majeure, according to people familiar with the situation. Rather than trying to walk away as the site’s main tenant, Oracle is attempting to put off payments should the data centre dubbed Project Jupiter get derailed and fail to come online in 2028 as planned, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private matters.

Companies typically invoke force majeure to free themselves from contractual obligations when problems arise beyond their control. In this case, Oracle is seeking to assert its contractual position if the build out is delayed. Still, it’s not certain that such a maneuver would free Oracle from its previously agreed financial obligations.

“Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule,” a spokesperson for Oracle said without commenting on the notice. “We are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward.”

A representative for Blue Owl, which owns the data-centre developer Stack Infrastructure, declined to comment.

The massive project in southern New Mexico is a major part of the Stargate AI infrastructure build-out that US President Donald Trump unveiled alongside leaders of Oracle, OpenAI and SoftBank Group Corp, serving as the marquee announcement in a series of US spending commitments that he touted in the early days of his second term. At the time, Trump called it a “tremendous investment” at a scale that “nobody’s really ever seen.”

See also: Cybersecurity stocks are so hot, investors question staying power

Almost two years later, the campus designed to handle 2.45 gigawatts — enough electricity to power roughly 1.8 million homes at any given moment — has hit serious setbacks including the denial of a permit key to its plans for energy resources. It’s becoming a symbol of the growing backlash against the broader AI data centre boom and a political flashpoint ahead of the US mid-term elections that threatens to turn races into referendums over the build-out.

Even if the force majeure notice is intended as a precautionary step to win some wiggle room, it risks alarming lenders backing the project. The debt tied to the development is already trading at stressed levels, below 90 cents on the dollar, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.

A group of about 20 banks provided an US$18 billion ($23 billion) loan to help fund the construction of the data centre campus, one of several mega-debt deals that have helped bankroll the AI infrastructure boom.

See also: BlackRock, IFM closing in on US$25 bil Asia data centre deal — Bloomberg

The notice also stands to raise questions yet again about the resilience of data centre leases. Contracts often include a clause allowing customers to back out if service doesn’t begin as scheduled. Earlier this year, Alphabet Inc’s Google agreed to pay Elon Musk’s SpaceX for computing power through mid-2029, for example, but reserved the right to terminate if it didn’t gain access by a certain date.

Force majeure provisions are relatively common in the energy and commodities world when events such as bad weather and geopolitical conflicts disrupt supplies, leaving companies unable to fulfill their contracts. The clauses are becoming more common in data centre developments as well, according to a recent client alert from Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan LLP.

“In AI data centre projects, force majeure is no longer a back-end boilerplate provision,” the June alert said. “It is a core litigation and risk-allocation tool that can determine whether a delay remains isolated — or cascades through the project’s construction, customer, power, insurance, and financing documents.”

OpenAI signed a US$400 billion deal with Oracle and SoftBank last year to support the development of five US data centres including the New Mexico site. Stack Infrastructure, a portfolio company of Blue Owl, is developing the facility, while Blue Owl itself has committed to providing equity.

A key natural gas pipeline project developed by Energy Transfer LP that was supposed to begin service this month and supply fuel to Project Jupiter was instead delayed by nearly six months to Feb 1, 2027, following repeated permit denials from the New Mexico State Land Office to approve a proposed route for the line. Project Jupiter is designed to be powered by gas-powered fuel cells from Bloom Energy Corp.

Oracle, for its part, has launched a charm offensive in New Mexico to counter the opposition. It remains unclear whether the company will win over the project’s skeptics.

Before Project Jupiter was revealed in full, the developers worked with local officials on an incentive plan and a strategy for how to roll out information to the public, according to documents previously reviewed by Bloomberg. Locals only learned the venture was tied to Oracle and OpenAI after it was approved.

title: Starbucks cuts 250 locations in North America to back higher-potential stores
article:
(Sept 24): Starbucks Corp is closing 250 underperforming locations across North America to focus on stores with higher potential.

The closures, which will happen this week, represent about 1% of the company’s 18,000-location footprint across the US and Canada. Starbucks has been pruning its portfolio as part of a broader push to bolster sales and profit, betting it can steer customers to locations that offer better service and stronger results. In the longer term, the company plans to resume expanding its footprint.

Starbucks “identified locations where we do not believe we can consistently deliver the experience we want for customers and partners or where we don’t see a path to acceptable financial performance”, chief operating officer Mike Grams said in a message to company employees.

The closures follow a separate round of closures announced last September, when Starbucks said it would shutter hundreds of North American stores as chief executive officer Brian Niccol moved to right-size the chain. The company targeted locations where it saw no path to profitability, while focusing on stores that aligned with Niccol’s push to make its cafes more inviting places to visit.

The company will incur US$300 million ($384 million) in restructuring charges from the latest store closures, according to a filing. Net openings for this fiscal year will be 440 locations, down from previous guidance of as many as 650.

Shares of Starbucks were little changed in pre-market trading on Thursday. The stock had gained about 12% this year through Wednesday, compared with a roughly 13% gain for the S&P 500.

See also: US Treasury to buy back up to US$6 bil in longer-dated govt debt

Starbucks has emerged from a sales slump in recent quarters after focusing on store upgrades, improved customer service, more relevant marketing and a revamped menu — all part of Niccol’s turnaround plan. Growth at established locations surpassed expectations last quarter, and analysts polled by Bloomberg expect the momentum to continue.

“This progress has given us a clearer view of the performance of every coffeehouse,” Grams wrote. Still, “while most are benefitting from this overall momentum, some coffeehouses continue to underperform despite the hard work and commitment of all of you”.

See also: US mortgage rates surge above 7% to a more than two-year high

Starbucks will offer transfers to workers at closing stores where possible. Those who can’t be reassigned will receive severance, according to the message.

The chain closed its latest fiscal year, ended Sept 28, 2025, with fewer stores in North America as it shuttered dozens of locations even as it opened hundreds of others.

Starbucks has said that it’s planning to rebuild its US store pipeline, seeking to open about 400 net new company-operated locations in its 2028 fiscal year. That excludes stores operated by partners such as grocery stores and airports. In the long run, Starbucks has said it could add at least 5,000 stores in the US alone.

“We are actively developing a strong pipeline of new coffeehouses and remain committed to growth in North America,” Grams wrote.

title: Trump says no moves towards AI guardrails in Xi summit
article:
(Sept 24): US President Donald Trump said he does not expect any moves to put guardrails around artificial intelligence (AI) during his summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

“A big day with President Xi of China. Super intelligence will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also,” Trump posted on his social media platform.

“Our guardrail is the DOJ!” he said, referring to the US Department of Justice.

International anxiety is rising about AI, with world leaders and AI labs warning that the technology could pose a danger to humanity if not developed safely.

In a speech before the United Nations this week, Trump dismissed calls for an international agreement to put guardrails around the development of AI. Trump said that existing institutions will be able to mitigate any risks.

title: IBF launches partnership with 23 banks, insurers and asset managers to redesign jobs in the age of AI
article:
The Institute of Banking and Finance (IBF) is partnering with financial institutions to assess the impact that AI will have on jobs before working together to trial new training approaches and redesign jobs.

The new partnership, titled the IBF AI Workforce Co-Lab, was announced by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) Gan Kim Yong at the IBF’s annual Distinction Evening on Sept 24. Gan, who is also the chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, was the guest of honour at the event.

“Financial institutions must plan for their people even as they plan for AI,” Gan told attendees. “The Co-Lab will bring employers and partners together to assess how jobs are changing, and test practical approaches to training and job redesign.”

The IBF AI Workforce Co-Lab brings together 23 financial institutions (FI) across Singapore’s banking, insurance and asset management sector. They comprise 13 banks, six insurers and four asset managers.

Participating FIs include both local and foreign banks such as DBS (SGX:D05 ) , Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation (OCBC) (SGX:O39 ) , United Overseas Bank (UOB) (SGX:U11 ) , UBS and JP Morgan; insurers such as Great Eastern, Prudential and Singlife; as well as asset managers Fullerton Fund Management, Millenium Capital, Schroders and the Singapore Exchange (SGX).

"We see AI’s true promise in empowering people – amplifying expertise, accelerating decision-making, and improving how work gets done," says Deep Thomas, JP Morgan Chase's Apac chief data and analytics officer. "That’s why we’re focused on enterprise AI tools, practical upskilling, and the guidance required to deploy AI responsibly at scale."

See also: EU answer to US banking deregulation triggers political pushback

Collectively, these 23 FIs account for about 40% of Singapore’s financial services workforce, or 80,000 employees. Gan says the FIs have committed to train their entire workforce in critical AI skills by 2028 through IBF-recognised programmes by 2028. To date, more than half of the employees at participating FIs have already completed the necessary training, Gan adds.

“This will give employees across different functions a common foundation for working with AI,” Gan says. “I encourage more financial institutions to join the Co-Lab and make this commitment to their people.”

IBF will use the findings derived from the Co-Lab to develop and launch three new career pathways for leaders within the financial services sector, wealth managers as well as operations professionals.

See also: BOE officials leave London for Leeds to set interest rates

AI will have a positive impact on the work of wealth managers and operations professionals, says Gan. Besides automating routine tasks, AI will free time up for them to focus on higher-value work such as client engagement and process improvement.

Lee Hwee Boon, head of group human resources at OCBC, says the Co-Lab builds on the bank's existing efforts to train their employees on AI-related skills. Aside from the three pathways IBF has launched, Lee says OCBC will be stepping up efforts to map our other pathways based the bank's skills-first growth and mobility strategy.

"In doing so, our colleagues can explore adjacent roles, acquire new skills, and pursue career growth within OCBC," Lee says.

Aside from the Co-Lab and new career pathways, Gan says the IBF will be launching three additional initiatives to help drive AI workforce transformation.

To provide business and human resource leaders with the necessary guidance on how AI adoption can affect jobs, IBF partnered with the Skills and Workforce Development Agency and the Institute for Human Resource Professionals to develop a Job Redesign Playbook for Financial Services.

In addition, IBF is working with Ngee Ann Polytechnic’s Centre for Shaping Human-First Transformation to provide skills mapping, coaching and change management resources to finance professionals navigating the disruption posed by AI.

Lastly, IBF is enhancing the existing tripartite MOU with the NTUC Financial and Professional Services Cluster of Unions as well as seven industry associations that span across banking, insurance, asset management, securities, financial advisory and FinTech.

“As AI adoption grows, some roles will expand, while others will change,” Gan says. “Developing our workforce must be part of this effort from the outset. We want AI to translate into better careers for Singaporeans and a more productive workforce.”
